frenchie:
How to tie a Frenchie. Lance Egan's jig-hook twist on the pheasant tail nymph gets down fast, rides point-up so it rarely snags, and the hot-spot collar seems to trigger strikes. It's a staple for Euro nymphing.

You'll need a barbless jig hook, size twelve to eighteen. A slotted tungsten bead in gold or copper. Brown eight-oh thread. Coq de Leon fibers for the tail, fine copper wire for the rib, pheasant tail fibers for the body, and hot pink or orange UV dubbing for the collar.

Step one. Slide the bead onto the hook, slot toward the bend. Add a few wraps of lead-free wire behind it if you want the fly heavier.

Step two. Start the thread and tie in a short tail of Coq de Leon fibers, then tie in the copper wire.

Step three. Tie in a few pheasant tail fibers by their tips and wrap them forward as the body. Rib them with the wire in open turns.

Step four. Right behind the bead, dub a small, bright collar of pink or orange. That's the hot spot.

Step five. Whip finish behind the bead and trim the thread.

Fish it on a tight-line Euro rig through riffles and runs. Because it rides point-up, you can bounce it along the bottom without hanging up.

san-juan-worm:
How to tie a San Juan Worm. Some anglers call it cheating, but trout eat aquatic worms all the time, and this simple pattern takes a couple of minutes to tie. It's one of the best flies to have when the water comes up after rain.

You'll need a curved scud hook, size eight to sixteen. Red six-oh thread. A short piece of red, pink or wine Vernille, also called ultra chenille. A tungsten bead is optional if you want it to sink faster.

Step one. Cut about two inches of Vernille and lightly flame both ends with a lighter, just enough to taper them like a worm.

Step two. Lay a thread base, then tie the Vernille on top at the middle of the shank.

Step three. Wrap the thread forward around the Vernille to the front of the hook, then back again, so it's locked down along the shank.

Step four. Whip finish. The two ends stick out front and back like a worm.

Fish it after rain, when the water rises and colors up and worms get washed in. Carp and panfish will eat it too.

rs2:
How to tie an RS2. Rim Chung's little emerger imitates a mayfly or midge just as it breaks out of its shuck. It's tiny and sparse, and it fools picky trout on tailwaters all over the country.

You'll need a fine-wire dry or emerger hook, size eighteen to twenty-four. Grey or black eight-oh thread. Two microfibbets for the tail. Grey beaver or another fine dubbing for the body, and a short tuft of grey CDC or white poly for the wing.

Step one. At the bend, tie in two microfibbets and split them apart with a few thread wraps between them.

Step two. Dub a slim, tapered body over about two-thirds of the shank. Use very little dubbing. Thin is the key.

Step three. On top of the shank, tie in a short tuft of CDC or poly, pointing back, as the emerging wing.

Step four. Dub a tiny thorax around the base of the wing, then whip finish.

Fish it in the film or just below it during a blue-winged olive hatch, or as a dropper under a small dry.

walts-worm:
How to tie a Walt's Worm. Walt Young's Pennsylvania pattern is just a bead and some hare's ear dubbing, but it looks like a cranefly larva, a caddis or a scud, and it catches fish everywhere.

You'll need a jig hook, size ten to eighteen. A silver or gold tungsten bead. Tan eight-oh thread, hare's ear dubbing, and fine wire if you want a rib.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start the thread right behind it, then wrap back to the bend.

Step two. Dub a carrot-shaped body of hare's ear, slim at the bend and thicker toward the bead.

Step three. Add a wire rib if you like, then whip finish. Finally, rough up the body with a piece of velcro so it looks buggy.

Fish it deep on a Euro rig. It's one of the best searching nymphs when nothing is hatching.

chubby-chernobyl:
How to tie a Chubby Chernobyl. This foam bug floats like a cork, carries a heavy nymph underneath, and passes for a hopper, a stonefly or a cicada. Guides in the West tie it on almost every day.

You'll need a two-X-long dry hook, size six to twelve. Tan three-oh thread. Ice Dub for the body, a strip of two-millimeter foam for the back, polypropylene or Widow's Web for the wing, and rubber legs.

Step one. Start the thread and dub a full, sparkly body of Ice Dub along the shank.

Step two. Lay the foam strip on top and tie it down at the rear and again near the front. Leave a little foam sticking out past the bend.

Step three. At the front tie-in point, add a wing of poly on top, and a pair of rubber legs on each side.

Step four. Trim the foam at the front, whip finish, and trim the legs to length.

It's the go-to float for a dry-dropper rig. Hang a nymph underneath and fish it along the banks.

griffiths-gnat:
How to tie a Griffith's Gnat. George Griffith's tiny dry looks like a cluster of midges, and when trout are sipping in slow water, it's often the only thing that works. It's quick to tie, even in small sizes.

You'll need a standard dry fly hook, size sixteen to twenty-four. Black eight-oh thread. Fine copper or gold wire for the rib, one or two strands of peacock herl, and a grizzly rooster hackle.

Step one. At the bend, tie in the fine wire, a grizzly hackle, and one or two strands of peacock herl.

Step two. Wind the peacock herl forward to the eye and tie it off.

Step three. Palmer the grizzly hackle forward in open turns and tie it off.

Step four. Wind the wire forward through the hackle to protect the herl, tie it off and whip finish.

Fish it when trout are sipping midges in slow water, and you can't match anything else. A light tippet helps.

daves-hopper:
How to tie a Dave's Hopper. Dave Whitlock's grasshopper has a yarn body, a turkey wing, knotted legs and a spun deer hair head. It takes some practice, but it's a beautiful fly and trout hammer it in late summer.

You'll need a two-X-long dry hook, size six to twelve. Yellow three-oh thread. Red deer hair for the tail. Yellow yarn and a brown hackle for the body. Mottled turkey quill for the wing, knotted grizzly hackle stems for the legs, and deer hair for the head.

Step one. At the bend, tie in a short tail of red deer hair, then a small loop of yellow yarn on top to extend the body.

Step two. Tie in a brown hackle, wrap the yarn body forward, and palmer the hackle over it. Then clip the hackle fibers short.

Step three. Tie in a slip of turkey quill on top as the wing, and a knotted leg on each side.

Step four. Spin a bunch or two of deer hair at the front for the collar and head. Whip finish, then clip the head to shape.

Slap it down near grassy banks on breezy summer afternoons. A little twitch can bring up big fish.

perdigon:
How to tie a Perdigon. These slim, resin-coated nymphs come from Spanish competition anglers. With no dubbing to slow them down, they sink like a stone, which makes them perfect for fast, deep water.

You'll need a jig hook, size twelve to eighteen. A slotted tungsten bead. Olive or brown eight-oh thread. Coq de Leon fibers for the tail, fine holographic tinsel for the rib, a black marker or hot-spot thread for the wing case, and thin UV resin.

Step one. Slide on the bead and start the thread. At the bend, tie in a short tail of Coq de Leon fibers.

Step two. Tie in the tinsel, wrap a slim, tapered thread body up to the bead, then rib it with the tinsel.

Step three. Color a wing case on top with a black marker, or wrap a small band of hot-spot thread behind the bead. Whip finish.

Step four. Coat the whole body with a thin layer of UV resin and cure it with a light.

Fish it on a Euro rig in fast, deep runs, where you need to get to the bottom in a hurry.

brassie:
How to tie a Brassie. This Colorado classic is just copper wire and a dark head, but it sinks fast and looks like a midge larva. It's one of the easiest flies there is, and one of the most effective on tailwaters.

You'll need a curved midge hook, size sixteen to twenty-two. Black eight-oh thread. Copper wire for the body, and muskrat or peacock dubbing for the head.

Step one. Start the thread and tie in the copper wire along the shank. Then wind the wire forward in tight, touching turns to make a smooth body, and tie it off near the eye.

Step two. Dub a small, dark head of muskrat or peacock right behind the eye.

Step three. Whip finish and trim the thread.

Fish it deep in tailwaters and slow runs, often as the dropper below a bigger nymph.

girdle-bug:
How to tie a Girdle Bug. This old western stonefly is just black chenille and white rubber legs, but its wiggling legs have fooled big trout for generations. It's fast to tie and nearly indestructible.

You'll need a three-X-long nymph hook, size four to ten. Black six-oh thread. Lead-free wire for weight, black chenille for the body, and white rubber legs.

Step one. Wrap lead-free wire around the middle of the shank, and cover it with thread so it stays put.

Step two. Tie in rubber legs at three points: a pair at the tail, a set at the middle, and a set near the front.

Step three. Wrap the chenille forward between the legs, tie it off behind the eye, and whip finish.

Dead-drift it deep through fast western runs, under an indicator or on a short line.
